questions.q: Who was Joseph Conrad, and what specific biographical fact explains the authentic maritime details in "Tomorrow"?
questions.a: Joseph Conrad (1857–1924) was a Polish-born British novelist who went to sea at 17, became a master mariner, and learned English in his 20s. His 16-year seafaring career — including command of a Congo River steamer and East-coast colliers — gives him firsthand knowledge of sailcloth suits, tarred twine, "soundings," and the psychology of men who "never got used to" the sea. A wrong answer (e.g., "He was an English poet") reveals the student lacks the biographical anchor to distinguish Conrad’s realism from romantic sea fiction.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the barber’s "judicious chaffing" fails to cure Captain Hagberd, using the story’s concept of "equilibrium based upon self-esteem."
questions.a: The barber assumes Hagberd’s delusion is a habit that can be teased away ("next week → next month → next year"). But Conrad writes: "Every mental state, even madness, has its equilibrium based upon self-esteem. Its disturbance causes unhappiness." Hagberd’s madness *is* his self-esteem — it structures his days (digging, buying furniture, advertising) and makes him "capable" and "hale." Chaffing threatens that structure, so Hagberd retreats into "puzzled and diffident" silence. A wrong answer (e.g., "The barber wasn’t funny enough") misses the psychological depth: the delusion is functional, not accidental.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "story within a story" to "Tomorrow": identify the three narrative layers and explain what each reveals about Hagberd that he would not say himself.
questions.a: Layer 1: The barber’s tap-room gossip (pp. 40–42) — reveals Hagberd’s arrival in mourning, his frantic search, the town’s mockery, and the barber’s cynical "cure." Layer 2: Hagberd’s own voice to Bessie (pp. 43–46) — reveals his emotional animosity to the sea, his domestic dream, and the shift from "next month" to "tomorrow." Layer 3: Harry’s return (pp. 52–68) — reveals the reality Hagberd fled: a son who despises domesticity, was beaten for wanting the sea, and returns only for money. Each layer strips away Hagberd’s self-mythology. A wrong answer that lists only plot events misses the *revelatory function* of each layer.

questions.q: Analyze the symbolism of the "No. 1 sailcloth suit" and the "spade" in relation to Hagberd’s identity. How do they represent his attempt to master two worlds he cannot control?
questions.a: The sailcloth suit — made secretly with tarred twine, worn "for the present" — is Hagberd’s attempt to *wear* the sea he hates but cannot leave; it makes him "a man roughened out of granite," a "deposed sea-god" who exchanged trident for spade. The spade turns his front garden into a "quagmire" — he digs "every day" but plants nothing "just at present," mirroring his endless preparation for a son who will never stay. Together, they symbolize a life suspended between a past he fled (sea) and a future he controls (land), both equally illusory. A wrong answer that calls them "clothes and a tool" misses the psychological symbolism Conrad builds through repetition and Bessie’s observations.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Bessie Carvil is the only sane person in the story." Use textual evidence to support or refute.
questions.a: Refute. Bessie *participates* in Hagberd’s delusion: she "half believes it herself," laughs at his winks, accepts his furniture descriptions, and never contradicts him — even when he says Harry will marry her. Her "informed silence which had an air of knowledge, expectation and desire" shows complicity. Meanwhile, Harry — though cynical and mercenary — sees the truth: "He wants his own way… He wants me to marry and settle." The barber, for all his mockery, diagnoses the mechanism: "equilibrium based upon self-esteem." Sanity in Conrad is not absence of delusion but awareness of it. Bessie’s final sob — "I don’t hear him any more" — confirms her entrapment. A wrong answer that calls her "kind" or "patient" confuses empathy with sanity.

questions.q: Create a one-paragraph "prologue" from the perspective of Hagberd’s wife (who died before the story opens) that explains *why* she was "impatient" and how her death triggered his move to Colebrook. Use only details implied in the text.
questions.a: A strong answer will: (1) adopt her voice — practical, weary, perhaps sharp; (2) reference the "bachelor uncle’s coal money" that freed them; (3) show her frustration with Hagberd’s "profound and emotional animosity" to the sea vs. his refusal to *act*; (4) imply she knew Harry was gone — "advertising for years" — and that her death left Hagberd without the only person who could say "stop"; (5) end with the letter/hoax that "brought him down" to Colebrook. A weak answer invents melodrama (illness, arguments) not grounded in Conrad’s restraint. The best answers capture Conrad’s irony: she died of "impatience" — the only thing that could break the cycle of "tomorrow."
